sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot v (printed pp. 37–44)
rows: [p. 37] [Margin: Nodus V. Substantiam aliquam liquidam esse superlunarem (continued at the head of p. 38).] Ereu. Ast ego tibi hoc polliceor si ex orbibus omne liquidum dempseris, statarios eos excursoribus efficere.

[p. 37] [Margin: Knot V. That some liquid substance [substantiam] is superlunar (continued at the head of p. 38).] Ereu. But I promise you this: if you take away from the orbs all liquid, [that you] make them stationary [statarios] [instead] of runners [excursoribus; or 'skirmishers'].

Et ne ludere tibi videar [p. 38] hoc primum vide. Sunto duo corpora A. et B. quae recte calleat mens nostra. Nonne vides quae de iis dicamus, eorum alia quidem non nisi singulis mutatis variari, alia vero immutato illo de quo loquimur variari posse.

And lest I seem to you to play, [p. 38] see this first. Let there be two bodies A. and B., which our mind may rightly be versed in [calleat]. Do you not see, [of the things] which we say about them, [that] of these some indeed are not varied unless the single [ones] [singulis] are changed, but others can be varied, that [thing] about which we speak being unchanged.

Ut quod A sit A, quaecumque mutatio in B fiat (si A maneat {?immotum}), semper verum erit. Quod autem A simile vel aequale sit ipsi B, quod ipsius causa vel effectus, prope vel remotum, simul vel alio tempore, et plura alia mutato B. mutari possunt, quantumvis A nihil detrimenti sit passum.

As, that A is A, whatever change may happen in B (if A remains unmoved [{?immotum}]), will always be true. But that A is like or equal to B itself, that [it is] its cause or effect, near or removed, at the same time or at another time, and many other [things], can be changed, B being changed, however much A has suffered nothing of detriment.

Vides ergo duas affirmatorum species, unam quae non nisi subiecto mutato diversificetur, aliam quae extrinseco aliquo mutato varietur. Nunc peto tertiamne credas esse dictorum progeniem quae nullo neque intrinseco neque extrinseco mutato variari possit?

You see therefore two species [species] of things affirmed [affirmatorum]: one which is not diversified unless the subject [subiecto] is changed, another which is varied, something extrinsic being changed. Now I ask whether you believe there to be a third offspring of things said [dictorum] which can be varied, nothing either intrinsic or extrinsic being changed?
Andab. Palam est non posse fieri.
Andab. It is plain [that it] cannot happen.

Asphal. Etiam ego tantumdem suspicor: sed si quid potes, Ereuni, aperi mihi intellectum, ut non opiner, sed omnino videam. Nisi enim memoria me fallat, non desunt nominati Philosophiae Magistri qui locum mutari, nulla facta neque in loco neque in locato intrinseca varietate, opinentur.

Asphal. I too suspect just as much; but if you can [do] anything, Ereunius, open the understanding [intellectum] to me, so that I may not opine [opiner], but altogether see. For unless memory deceives me, there are not lacking named Masters of Philosophy who opine [opinentur] that place is changed, no intrinsic variety having been made either in the place or in the [thing] placed [locato].

[Margin: Nullo intrinseco mutato extrinsecum non mutari.] Ereu. Sic est, sed numquid hoc principio evidentius aliud est, Quod idem si non est mutatum manet idem? Et si hoc verum est de sin- [p. 39] gulis nonne etiam de pluribus? ut si A immutatum semper sit A, etiam A, B immutata semper sint A, B.

[Margin: That, nothing intrinsic being changed, the extrinsic [extrinsecum] is not changed.] Ereu. So it is; but is anything else more evident than this principle [principio]: That the same, if it is not changed, remains the same? And if this is true of single [things], [p. 39] [is it] not also of more [than one] [pluribus]? as, if A unchanged is always A, also A, B unchanged are always A, B.
Et eadem evidentia firmum est si A et B sint, et A aliquid vel sit vel operetur circa B, manentibus iisdem omnibus idem semper A sive esse sive operari circa B.

And by the same evidence [evidentia] it is firm [that], if A and B are, and A either is or operates something about [circa] B, all [things] remaining the same, A always either is or operates the same about B.

Nunc itaque esto A locus et locatum B: si A neque B in sese aliquam mutationem subeat, fit semper A esse A et B, B: sed et A respectu B idem semper esse et operari. Si itaque erat aliquando A et B, et A non locabat B, donec omnia eadem manent, impossibile est ut A locet B: Et si semel locus fuerit; impossibile erit iisdem statibus, non esse eiusdem locum.

Now therefore let A be the place and B the [thing] placed: if [neither] A nor B undergoes any change in itself, it comes about [fit] that A always is A and B, B; but also [that] A in respect of [respectu] B always is and operates the same. If therefore there was at some time A and B, and A was not placing [locabat] B, as long as all [things] remain the same, it is impossible that A place B; and if once it has been the place, it will be impossible, the same states [statibus] [remaining], [for it] not to be the place of the same.

Asphal. Sed cur non etiam hoc inter contingentia collocetur, ut A et B aliquam inter se denominationem mutent ex tertii alicuius mutatione? Sortes et Callias sunt concives, iis intactis, destructae sint Athenae, nonne vides non amplius esse concives?

Asphal. But why should not this too be placed among contingent [things] [contingentia]: that A and B change some denomination [denominationem] between themselves from the change of some third [thing]? Sortes and Callias are fellow-citizens; they being untouched, let Athens have been destroyed [destructae sint]: do you not see [that they] are no longer fellow-citizens?

Ereu. Video, Asphali, contingere ut dicis, neque dubito in natura extare paria, si investigandi necessitas ulla foret; neque nos duo ita posuimus, ut plura excluderemus, sed ut in brevi numero quanticumque rationem expediremus; unde et omnibus iisdem manentibus in expositione posuimus.

Ereu. I see, Asphalius, [that it] happens [contingere] as you say, nor do I doubt that like [cases] [paria] stand forth [extare] in nature, if there were any necessity of investigating; nor did we put two [bodies] so as to exclude more, but so as to set out [expediremus] in a short number the reason [rationem] of however many [quanticumque; lit. 'of however great']; whence also we put in the exposition [expositione] 'all [things] remaining the same'.

Si vides igitur nullo in se mutato non posse contingere ut respectus unius ad aliud varietur, cum respec- [p. 40] tus non aliud sit quam quid unum sit si comparetur alteri; ubicumque autem nihil in se mutatum est, necessum esse unum respectu alterius semper idem esse quod fuit, et quod inde sequitur, extrinseca non mutari si nulla sit intrinseca mutatio, ad Andabatam me converto et sic infero.

If therefore you see [that], nothing being changed in itself, it cannot happen that the respect [respectus] of one to another is varied, since a respect [p. 40] is not other than what one [thing] is if it is compared to another; but [that] wherever nothing is changed in itself, it is necessary that one in respect of another always is the same which it was, and, what follows thence, [that] extrinsic [things] are not changed if there is no intrinsic change: [then] I turn myself to Andabata and infer thus.

Si duae contiguae sphaerae adeo solidae sint, ut ex neutra quicquam deteri possit per motum, nihil est intrinsecum quod in iis per motum localem mutari possit. Si ponitur itaque mutari localiter coelum, ponitur extrinsece, i[d est]. secundum locum mutatio facta, cum nulla res in sese variata esse credatur.

If two contiguous spheres are so solid that from neither can anything be rubbed away [deteri] through motion, there is nothing intrinsic which can be changed in them through local motion. If therefore the heaven is posited to be changed locally, a change is posited made extrinsically [extrinsece], that is, according to place, since no thing is believed to have been varied in itself.

Vide Andabata si quid habes quo vel assumptorum aliquod infirmes, vel inconsequentiam latere suadeas, aut ingenue fatere irrefragabiliter etiam hoc confectum esse, corpus aliquod divisibile supra lunam et in illo immortalium substantiarum choro esse compertum.

See, Andabata, if you have anything by which you may either weaken some [one] of the [things] assumed [assumptorum], or persuade [that] an inconsequence [inconsequentiam] lies hid; or frankly confess [that] this too has been irrefragably made out [confectum]: [that] some divisible body has been found [compertum] above the moon, and in that choir of immortal substances.

Andab. Scio magistros ad ubicationum recurrere suffugia. Sed quoniam iis decessi, factam semel fidem irritare non sustineo. Sed quid ingentis rei habes, si divisibile corpus in coelis fateri coegisti, cum non desint Theologorum vel Coryphaei in omnium immortalium corporum principe Coelo quod Empyreum vocant, similem divisibilitatem collocantes?

Andab. I know [that] the masters run back to the refuges [suffugia] of ubications [ubicationum]. But since I have withdrawn from them [iis decessi], I cannot bear to make void [irritare] a pledge [fidem] once made. But what of a huge thing [ingentis rei] do you have, if you have compelled [me] to confess a divisible body in the heavens, since there are not lacking even [vel] Coryphaei of the Theologians placing a like divisibility in the prince of all immortal bodies, the Heaven which they call Empyrean?

[p. 41] [Margin: Substantiam mortalem in Coelis reperiri.] Ereu. Neque quicquam magni promisisse memini. Tu modo ad hoc adverte animum, num quod divisibile est et divisioni perpetuo subiectum, eiusmodi sit, ut immortalitatis honore dignum sit?

[p. 41] [Margin: That a mortal substance is found in the Heavens.] Ereu. Nor do I remember [that I] promised anything great. Do you only turn [your] mind to this: whether what is divisible and perpetually subject to division is of such a kind that it is worthy of the honour of immortality?
Quid enim ex his ambigis? quod individuo mutatur, interire quod dividatur (de homogeneis loquor) individuum mutare, vel tandem quod interire potest, mortale esse dicendum.

For what of these do you waver about [ambigis]? [that] what is changed in [its] individual [individuo], perishes; [that] what is divided (I speak of homogeneous [things]), changes [its] individual [individuum]; or finally [that] what can perish must be called mortal.
Quod si nihil horum extimescis, vide non divisibile dumtaxat; sed et mortale corpus tuis immortalibus illatum.
But if you fear none of these, see [that] not only a divisible, but also a mortal body [has been] brought in among [illatum] your immortals.

Neque quicquam promovet Theologorum allegata sententia, nisi hoc diserte expresserint quam immortalitatis rationem in Empyreo constituere intendant, si quidem et si plures immortalitatis notiones esse possint, nos eas solas, quae instituto quod prae manibus est inserviunt usurpabimus.

Nor does the alleged opinion [sententia] of the Theologians advance anything, unless they have expressly [diserte] expressed this: what reason [rationem] of immortality they intend to establish in the Empyrean; since indeed, even if there can be more notions [notiones] of immortality, we shall use [usurpabimus] those alone which serve the purpose [instituto] which is in hand.

Sunt autem duae: aliud enim habet ex sese unde destructioni repugnet, aliud non ex sese quidem, sed ex circumstantibus idem obtinere possit. Tu modo edissere utrum genus coelo a Philosophis accommodatum credas.

And they are two: for one [thing] has from itself [that] whence it is repugnant to [repugnet] destruction; another can obtain the same, not indeed from itself, but from the [things] standing around [circumstantibus]. Do you only set forth which kind you believe [was] accommodated to the heaven by the Philosophers.

Andab. Prius citra dubium. Non eo dumtaxat titulo quod nobilius et efficacius est; sed quod inter formam coeli et materiam, tam indissolubilem connexionem asserant, ut vel nullius praeterea formae capax sit materia, vel si sit, certe hac forma adeo satiata sit, ut quan- [p. 42] tumvis ex sese alius sit capax: totus tamen ille appetitus, huius receptione deferbuerit.

Andab. The former, without doubt. Not by that title [titulo] only, that it is nobler and more efficacious; but because they assert so indissoluble a connexion between the form of the heaven and the matter, that either the matter is capable of no form besides, or, if it is, it is certainly so sated by this form that, however much [p. 42] it is of itself capable of another, yet that whole appetite [appetitus] has cooled down [deferbuerit] by the reception of this [form].
Tum etiam, nisi ex sese esset immortale (ex intrinsecis inquam) ab elementari mundo adeo coniuncto et circumlato, necessario pateretur.
Then also, unless it were immortal from itself (from intrinsic [things], I say), it would necessarily suffer from the elementary world, so conjoined and carried around [circumlato].

Ereu. Hoc itaque vide quale sit. Divisibilitatem iam vides idem valere, quod destruibilitatem: unde Coelum tuum duas habet rationes (quae quomodo in unum conveniant, tuum est docere) ex una scilicet parte non posse destrui, hoc est, non posse dividi; ex alia parte aptum natum esse dividi, hoc est destrui.

Ereu. See therefore of what sort this is. You now see [that] divisibility is equivalent [valere] to the same [idem] as destructibility: whence your Heaven has two reasons [rationes] (how these come together into one, it is yours to teach): namely on the one part, not to be able to be destroyed, that is, not to be able to be divided; on the other part, to be apt by nature [aptum natum] to be divided, that is, destroyed.

Et quoniam hoc posterius evidens est, ut pote oculis ipsis aspectabile (non enim aliis opus est testibus, ut quantitatem coeli astruamus) ignotum illud, et suspicione nixum relegandum ego arbitrer, nisi tuum expectem suffragium.

And since this latter is evident, as being visible to the eyes themselves (for there is no need of other witnesses, that we may build up [astruamus] the quantity of the heaven), I would judge that unknown [one], and [one] resting on suspicion, to be relegated, did I not await your vote [suffragium].

Andab. Ast ego nihil temere ausim; sed duplex tuis telis obiicio scutum. Hoc primo. Quanti rationem non in divisibilitate, sed in impenetrabilitate, mensura, vel alio aliquo ex multis, de quibus in scholis litigatur, constituendam esse. Deinde partes quanti unius separabiles re ipsa esse, posse tamen alterius sola mente designabiles comperiri. His stantibus, frustra paeana cecineris.

Andab. But I would dare nothing rashly; but I throw a double shield against your weapons. This firstly: that the reason [rationem] of a quantum [Quanti] is to be established not in divisibility, but in impenetrability, measure, or some other out of the many about which there is litigation in the schools. Next, that the parts of one quantum are separable in the thing itself [re ipsa], [but] those of another can nevertheless be found designable by the mind alone. These standing, you will have sung the paean in vain.

[Margin: Quantitatem esse idem quod divisibilitatem (continued at the head of p. 43).] Ereu. Excidit proinde tibi quod dum de [p. 43] loco ageremus, de summis decem generibus universim pronunciavimus; nempe eorum notiones a natura esse, et omnium gentium communes: neque ex doctis laboribus; sed ex simplici generis humani sensu trahendas esse.

[Margin: That quantity is the same as divisibility (continued at the head of p. 43).] Ereu. It has therefore slipped from you [Excidit … tibi] what, while we were treating of [p. 43] place, we pronounced universally [universim] about the highest ten kinds [summis decem generibus]: namely that their notions [notiones] are from nature, and common to all nations; and are to be drawn not from learned labours, but from the simple sense of the human race.

Vide ergo cum hi rudes aliquid quantum sit petunt, num non per mensuram, quae saepius repetita rem, de qua quaeritur, adaequet, plerumque respondeatur? Vide num per passus ulnas, libras et similia, non satisfiat interroganti:

See therefore, when these rude [people] ask how great [quantum] something is, whether it is not for the most part answered through a measure which, repeated more often, equals [adaequet] the thing about which it is asked? See whether the one asking is not satisfied through paces, ells, pounds and the like:

Et si per haec quieta sit, quae dubia erat mens, agnosce definitionem partis, quae repetita metiatur totum, et de partibus agi cum de magnitudine quaeritur, quicquid magistri tui disputent, intellige.

And if through these the mind which was doubtful is quieted, acknowledge the definition of a part, [namely that] which, repeated, measures the whole; and understand that it is a matter of [agi de] parts when it is asked about magnitude, whatever your masters may dispute.

[Margin: Omnis quantitatis partes esse separabiles.] Quam autem subintulisti partium distinctionem, ut aliae sint signabiles, aliae vero separabiles; Ea mihi hoc arguere videtur, corpora aliqua in rerum natura esse ut ipsi conducant, alia vero tantummodo ut spectentur ab hominibus.

[Margin: That the parts of every quantity are separable.] But the distinction of parts which you brought in underneath [subintulisti], that some are signable, but others separable: this seems to me to argue [arguere] this, that some bodies are in the nature of things that they may be of profit to themselves [ipsi], but others only that they may be looked at by men.
Quale enim est hoc quod asseris esse quantitatem, cuius partes sint tantummodo signabiles? nisi esse quantitatem, cuius ratio sit, esse divisibilem a mente?
For of what sort is this which you assert to be a quantity, whose parts are only signable? unless [it is] to be a quantity whose reason [ratio] is to be divisible by the mind?

Cum itaque divisibilitas (ut ipso nomine patet) passibilitas quaedam sit, huius quantitatis ratio est, ut a ratione pati possit. i[d est]. ut fingi seu concipi possit esse divisum; non autem ut ipsa re, divisa esse possit:

Since therefore divisibility (as is plain from the name itself) is a certain passibility [passibilitas], the reason [ratio] of this quantity is that it can suffer from reason [a ratione], that is, that it can be feigned or conceived to be divided, but not that in the thing itself [ipsa re] it can be divided:

quod est, ac si totidem verbis et scholae vocibus dicamus, aliam esse [p. 44] quantitatem rationis, aliam rei: seu unam esse veram et existentem, aliam fictam et imaginariam, et vere nullam. Habes ergo (si quid ego intelligo) perforata quae, obiecisti, scuta.

which is as if we should say in so many words and with the words [vocibus] of the school, that one is [p. 44] a quantity of reason [rationis], another of the thing [rei]; or that one is true and existing, the other feigned and imaginary, and truly none. You have therefore (if I understand anything) the shields which you threw against [me] pierced through.

terms: Military: miles statarius is the soldier who fights standing in line, excursores are light skirmishers who run out. 'excursoribus' (printed as one word) can be read as 'ex cursoribus' ('from runners') or as the noun 'skirmishers'.
The image is of the celestial orbs as troops: without a fluid medium they could not move, and would become 'stationary' instead of 'running' (cursus is also the astronomical 'course').
White insists that the mind fully grasps the two bodies A and B, so the argument is about clear notions.

White classifies predicates: intrinsic (changing only when the subject changes) and extrinsic (changing when something else changes); a scholastic distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic denomination.
'the thing underlying'; logical subject of predication or physical substrate.
Both senses are in play: the subject of the statements is the body itself.

Scholastic denominatio extrinseca: a predicate a thing receives from a relation to something outside it (Sortes and Callias are no longer fellow-citizens once Athens is destroyed). Asphalius' objection is the classic 'Cambridge change'.
Standard name in scholastic logical examples (Sortes et Plato); Callias is Aristotle's stock example name.
Scholastic term for a relation (respectus = relatio). White defines it as 'what one thing is if it is compared to another', i.e. relations supervene on their terms.
Aristotelian place (locus) and the body in place (locatum). White argues that place cannot change unless something intrinsic in container or contained changes.
From detero. If two solid spheres rub with nothing worn away, local motion changes nothing intrinsic in them, which White's principle makes impossible; so a fluid must lie between them.
Printed 'extrinsece' (adverb); see the extrinsic/intrinsic distinction above.
Logical: that the conclusion does not follow from the premises (assumpta).
Scholastic mode of 'where' (ubi) intrinsic to a body; Andabata had given up this refuge in Knot iv. Already in the glossary.
irritus = void (legal); a scholastic disputant must keep concessions made.
'leaders of the chorus', i.e. leading figures.
Greek κορυφαῖος, the leader of a chorus; used of leading scholars. Echoes 'choro' (the 'choir of immortal substances') just before.
The outermost, unmoving heaven of medieval theology, seat of the blessed; some theologians gave it divisible parts (it contains bodies of the blessed).
White's chain: what is divided (if homogeneous) becomes other individuals; what changes its individual perishes; what can perish is mortal. Hence divisible = destructible.
Aristotelian homoeomerous bodies, whose parts are of the same nature as the whole (so division makes two new individuals of the same kind).
Classical sense of usurpare: to make use of a term.
Scholastic: a nature that of itself excludes destruction (intrinsic incorruptibility) vs. one preserved by its surroundings.
Kept literal (participle) to keep White's contrast ex sese / ex circumstantibus.

Aristotelian-scholastic doctrine that prime matter 'desires' form (Phys. I.9, 192a22). The scholastic view: celestial matter is so sated with its form that it has no appetite for another, hence the heavens are incorruptible.
Metaphor of the appetite of matter cooling off.
'the world of the four elements', 'sublunary world'.
Aristotelian division between the sublunary (elemental) and celestial regions.
Scholastic aptus natus (= Greek πεφυκός): having a natural capacity.
Late and scholastic sense 'establish by argument'; lit. 'build on'.
Roman voting term; Ereunius courteously defers to Andabata.
a quantum / reason of a quantum
Scholastic debate on the essence of quantity: divisibility, impenetrability, extension, measure, etc. White holds it is divisibility into parts.
The Thomist doctrine that the parts of the heavens are only mentally 'signable'; White rejects a quantity whose parts can only be marked off by the mind as a 'quantity of reason'.
Classical allusion: the paean as a song of triumph.
Aristotle's categories, whose notions White says come from common human sense (cf. Knot iv).
White plays on 'divisibility' (-bilitas, a capacity of undergoing) and 'pati a ratione', 'to suffer from reason'.
quantity of reason / of the thing
Scholastic ens rationis vs. ens reale.
vox in its logical sense (as glossary).
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot v, complete in one part. PDF pp. 48–55 = printed pp. 37–44. It begins at the foot of p. 37 with Ereunius' 'Ast ego tibi hoc polliceor' (margin 'Nodus V. Substantiam aliquam liquidam esse superlunarem', running onto p. 38), although FM2's table gives p. 38. It ends on p. 44 with Ereunius' '…perforata quae, obiecisti, scuta.'; Asphalius' 'Etiam hoc, Ereuni, nobis aperi' begins Knot vi on p. 44 (margin 'Nodus VI. Unde invaluerit de orbibus coelestibus opinio'), as FM2 says. The offset of +11 holds (p. 44 = PDF 55).

Rows: one row per speech, with long speeches by Ereunius split at sentence breaks; printed page breaks are marked [p. n] where they fall, including mid-word ('sin- [p. 39] gulis'). Marginal notes: 'Nodus V. Substantiam aliquam liquidam esse superlunarem' (pp. 37–38), 'Nullo intrinseco mutato extrinsecum non mutari' (p. 38), 'Substantiam mortalem in Coelis reperiri' (p. 41), 'Quantitatem esse idem quod divisibilitatem' (pp. 42–43), 'Omnis quantitatis partes esse separabiles' (p. 43).

Conventions as in glossary.md: long s → s; æ/œ → ae/oe; tildes expanded (mutationẽ → mutationem); 'i.' expanded as i[d est]; consonantal u → v; accents dropped; '&' → et. Spellings kept as printed: 'coelum', 'obiicio', 'pronunciavimus', 'expectem', 'necessum', 'extrinsece', 'alius' (genitive, p. 42), 'ut pote'.

Printed/sense notes: (a) p. 37, 'excursoribus' is printed as one word; it may be 'ex cursoribus' ('out of runners'); both give the same sense (see terms). (b) p. 38, 'imo tum' is printed with a gap and a missing letter; read 'immotum' (it could also be 'immutatum', which the argument would suit, but the letters fit 'immotum'). (c) p. 39, 'fit semper A esse A & B,B' is punctuated 'A esse A, et B, B'. (d) p. 41, 'quod individuo mutatur, interire quod dividatur … individuum mutare' lacks punctuation between the clauses; read as three propositions. (e) p. 44, 'aliam r϶i' has a damaged letter; read 'rei'. (f) p. 44, the comma in 'quae, obiecisti' is kept as printed.

Uncertain: {?immotum} (p. 38). 'quanticumque' (p. 39) is read as the genitive of quantuscumque ('of however great [a number]'); the sense is 'to set out the reasoning for any number of bodies'. No illegible words.

Verification pass: the transcription was compared again with the page images (300 dpi crops of the foot of p. 37 and the margin of p. 38), and the English with the Latin, sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, negatives, comparatives, omissions). This gave 4 corrections: (1) p. 39, 'si A neque B … subeat' had been rendered 'if A nor B'; '[neither]' supplied. (2) p. 39, 'destructae sint Athenae' (perfect subjunctive) had been rendered 'let Athens be destroyed'; corrected to 'let Athens have been destroyed'. (3) p. 41, 'Quid enim ex his ambigis?' had been rendered 'which of these'; corrected to the literal 'what of these'. (4) p. 42, 'idem valere, quod destruibilitatem' had been rendered loosely; now 'is equivalent to the same [idem] as', with the Latin bracketed. Transcription: no changes; 'immotum' (p. 38) remains uncertain.
